q: A transformer works on the principle of:
explanation: An alternating flux produced by the primary links the secondary and induces an EMF in it (Faraday’s law) — mutual induction.
why: Electrostatic induction is the capacitor principle.
Hall effect is used in sensors, not transformers.
Self induction alone cannot transfer energy to a second winding.

q: The open-circuit (no-load) test on a transformer is used to determine:
explanation: With the secondary open, current is only the small no-load current, so copper loss is negligible and the wattmeter reads core (iron) loss. It also gives R_{0} and X_{0} of the shunt branch.
why: Regulation needs SC test data (R_{eq}, X_{eq}).
Copper loss is measured in the short-circuit test.
Equivalent series resistance comes from the SC test.

q: The short-circuit test on a transformer gives:
explanation: At rated current the applied voltage is only 5–10% of rated, so the flux and iron loss are negligible: the wattmeter reads full-load copper loss. Also gives Z_{eq}, R_{eq}, X_{eq}.
why: Hysteresis is part of iron loss, negligible here.
Eddy loss is part of iron loss, negligible here.
Iron loss is negligible at the reduced SC voltage.

q: The open-circuit test is normally performed on the ___ side and the short-circuit test on the ___ side.
explanation: OC test needs rated voltage — easier to supply on the LV side. SC test needs rated current — smaller on the HV side, and only a small voltage is needed.
why: SC on LV needs very large rated current.
Reversed: rated HV voltage for OC would need a costly HV source.
SC on HV is right, but OC on HV is impractical.

q: Buchholz relay is used to protect:
explanation: Buchholz is a gas-actuated relay for oil-immersed transformers (typically above ~500 kVA). Slow gas build-up from incipient faults sounds an alarm; a sudden oil surge trips the breaker.
why: Lines use distance and overcurrent relays.
Motors use thermal overload and other relays.
Alternators use differential, loss-of-excitation and similar relays.

q: Buchholz relay is installed:
options: At the bottom of the tank
In the pipe between the main tank and the conservator
explanation: It sits in the connecting pipe so that gas rising from the tank collects in it before reaching the conservator.
why: Gas rises upward and would not collect at the bottom.
Bushings carry the conductors out of the tank.
The breather dries air entering the conservator.

q: The breather of a transformer contains:
explanation: Silica gel absorbs moisture from air drawn into the conservator as oil contracts. Typical silica gel turns from blue (dry) to pink (saturated) and must then be replaced or reactivated.
why: SF6 is used in breakers and GIS.
Carbon is not a desiccant here.
Oil is in the tank and conservator, not the breather.

q: The main function of the conservator in a transformer is to:
options: Allow for expansion and contraction of oil
explanation: The conservator keeps the main tank full of oil while oil volume changes with temperature and minimises oil surface exposed to air.
why: Eddy loss is reduced by laminations.
Cooling is by radiators/fans.
Fault detection is the Buchholz relay’s job.

q: The core of a transformer is laminated mainly to reduce:
explanation: Thin insulated laminations break the path of circulating eddy currents (eddy loss ∝ t^{2}). Silicon content in steel reduces hysteresis loss.
why: Copper loss is in the windings.
Leakage reactance depends on winding arrangement.
Hysteresis loss is reduced by using silicon (CRGO) steel.

q: Hysteresis loss in a transformer core varies with frequency f and maximum flux density B_{m} as:
explanation: Steinmetz: P_{h} = η B_{m}^{1.6} f V. Eddy loss P_{e} ∝ B_{m}^{2} f^{2} t^{2}.
why: That is the eddy-current loss relation.
Not a standard relation.
Hysteresis loss is proportional to frequency.

q: Transformer ratings are given in kVA rather than kW because:
options: Losses depend on voltage and current, not on load power factor
kW is not an SI unit
explanation: Iron loss depends on voltage, copper loss on current. Neither depends on the load pf, so the rating is in VA.
why: Transformers do have losses.
kW is an SI-derived unit.
They supply both real and reactive power.

q: A transformer has maximum efficiency when:
options: Load is at unity pf and full load always
explanation: Efficiency is maximum when variable (copper) loss equals constant (iron) loss.
why: That is not the condition for dη/dI = 0.
Iron loss is never zero in operation.
Max efficiency load depends on the loss ratio, not always full load.

q: A transformer has 2200 V primary with 1000 turns. For a 220 V secondary the number of secondary turns is:
explanation: = 100 turns
why: Ratio applied twice.
Equal turns give equal voltage.
That would step up to 22 kV.

q: A 10 kVA, 2000/200 V single-phase transformer. Full-load secondary current is:
explanation: = 50 A (primary is 5 A)
why: Off by a factor of 10.
That is the primary current.
Not consistent with 10 kVA at 200 V.

q: A 20 kVA transformer has iron loss 200 W and full-load copper loss 500 W. Efficiency at full load, 0.8 pf is about:
why: 20000/20700 — assumes unity pf.
16000/16200 — ignores copper loss.
16000/16500 — ignores iron loss.

q: Iron loss = 400 W and full-load copper loss = 900 W. Maximum efficiency occurs at what fraction of full load?
explanation: ≈ 66.7% of full load
why: 12% higher than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.
Only if iron loss equals full-load copper loss.
400/900 without the square root.

q: Full-load copper loss of a transformer is 800 W. Copper loss at half load is:
why: Assumes copper loss ∝ I, not I².
Copper loss changes with load.
That is ⅛ of full load.

q: Voltage regulation of a transformer can be negative when the load power factor is:
explanation: With a sufficiently leading load, the capacitive current raises the secondary voltage above no-load value (Ferranti-like rise), giving negative regulation.
why: Zero-lag pf gives maximum positive regulation.
At unity pf regulation is small but positive.
Lagging loads give the largest positive regulation.

q: A transformer secondary reads 240 V at no load and 230 V at full load. Percentage regulation (referred to full-load voltage) is about:
why: 10/240 — referred to no-load voltage.
Volts, not percentage.
52% lower than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.

q: All-day efficiency is an important figure of merit for:
explanation: Distribution transformers are energised 24 h but lightly loaded much of the time, so energy efficiency over a day (kWh out/kWh in) matters. They are designed for maximum efficiency at a lower load.
why: Accuracy matters for instrument transformers.
Welding transformers are intermittent duty; not the standard example.
Power transformers run near full load; ordinary efficiency suits them.

q: If a transformer primary is connected to a DC supply of rated voltage:
options: The primary draws very high current and may burn
explanation: With DC there is no changing flux, so no back EMF; only the small winding resistance limits current, which becomes very large.
why: No induced EMF with DC.
No EMF is induced in the secondary.
A transformer cannot rectify.

q: On-load tap changers are usually placed on the HV winding because:
options: HV winding has more turns and lower current
HV winding is at the bottom
explanation: Lower current reduces arcing and contact size; more turns give finer voltage steps.
why: Physical position is not the reason.
Taps can be provided on either side.
Taps do not affect iron loss meaningfully.

q: An auto-transformer has a ratio 400/300 V. The saving of copper compared with a two-winding transformer of the same output is:
solution: Copper in auto = (1 − K) × copper in two-winding = 0.25
explanation: Saving = K = 75%
why: 25% is the copper still needed.
56% lower than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.
33% lower than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.

q: Which condition is NOT essential for parallel operation of two single-phase transformers?
explanation: Transformers of different kVA ratings can share load in proportion to their ratings if their per-unit impedances are equal. Polarity and ratio must match.
why: Unequal p.u. impedance causes poor load sharing.
Wrong polarity gives a dead short circulating current.
Unequal ratios cause circulating currents at no load.

q: In a DC generator, the commutator:
options: Converts the AC induced in the armature to DC at the brushes
explanation: EMF induced in armature conductors is alternating; the commutator with brushes acts as a mechanical rectifier.
why: Interpoles/compensating windings reduce armature reaction effects.
The field winding provides excitation.
Voltage depends on flux, speed and winding, not the commutator.

q: A 4-pole lap-wound DC generator has 500 conductors, flux 0.02 Wb/pole and runs at 1200 rpm. Generated EMF is:
why: Uses A = 2 (wave winding).
Ignores the parallel paths entirely.
Halves the correct value.

q: A 220 V DC shunt motor has armature resistance 0.5 Ω and takes armature current 20 A. Back EMF is:
why: Uses a 1 Ω drop.
Ignores the armature drop.
Adds the drop — that is a generator relation.

q: A DC series motor should never be started at no load because:
explanation: Speed ∝ 1/φ and φ ∝ I_{a}; at no load I_{a} and flux are tiny, so speed rises dangerously. Series motors are always coupled to the load (traction, cranes).
why: Starting current is high, not low.
No such effect.
It starts with very high torque.

q: Which DC motor is most suitable for electric traction?
explanation: Series motors give very high starting torque (T ∝ I_{a}^{2} below saturation) and naturally slow down under heavy load.
why: Differential compound is unstable and rarely used.
Shunt motors are near-constant speed with moderate starting torque.
Used for wide speed control, not classic traction.

q: A DC shunt motor is best described as a:
explanation: Flux is nearly constant (field across supply), so speed drops only slightly from no load to full load.
why: Series motors vary speed widely with load.
Series motors have the highest starting torque.
Universal motors are series motors that run on AC or DC.

q: A DC shunt motor runs at 1000 rpm. If the field flux is reduced by 10% with back EMF unchanged, the new speed is about:
why: 1100 assumes N ∝ (2 − φ); speed is inversely proportional.
Speed rises, not falls, when flux is weakened.
Flux change does change speed.

q: Swinburne's test cannot be performed on a DC series motor because:
options: Running a series motor at no load is unsafe
explanation: Swinburne's is a no-load test: a series motor at no load runs away. It is used for shunt and compound machines.
why: A series motor has a series field winding.
That is Hopkinson's (regenerative) test.
All motors have losses.

q: Interpoles in DC machines are provided to:
explanation: Interpoles (commutating poles), connected in series with the armature, neutralise reactance voltage and armature reaction in the commutating zone, reducing sparking.
why: Hysteresis depends on core material.
They act locally in the commutating zone only.
They do not set speed.

q: In a 3-point starter for a DC shunt motor, the no-volt release coil is connected:
options: In series with the shunt field
In parallel with the armature only
explanation: The hold-on coil is in series with the field: if supply fails or the field opens, the arm returns to OFF, protecting against runaway on field loss.
why: The overload release is in the line/armature circuit.
Not its connection.
Not its connection.

q: Synchronous speed of a 4-pole induction motor on a 50 Hz supply is:
why: That is 2 poles.
That is 8 poles.
That is 6 poles.

q: A 6-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at 960 rpm. Its slip is:
why: Uses 980 rpm.
50% higher than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.
Mixes fraction and percentage.

q: An induction motor on 50 Hz runs at 4% slip. Frequency of rotor currents is:
explanation: = 2 Hz
why: Forgets to multiply by f.
That is the stator frequency (true only at standstill).
That is (1 − s)f.

q: A 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor operates at 3% slip. Rotor speed is:
why: That is 2% slip.
That is synchronous speed.
Adds the slip; motors run below N_{s}.

q: Air-gap power of an induction motor is 10 kW at slip 0.04. Rotor copper loss is:
explanation: = 400 W (mechanical power developed = 9.6 kW)
why: 140% higher than the correct result — does not follow from the correct working.
That is gross mechanical power (1 − s)P_{g}.
Off by 10.

q: In a 3-phase induction motor, maximum torque is:
explanation: T_{max} ∝ V^{2}/(2X_{2}); rotor resistance only changes the slip at which it occurs (s_{m} = R_{2}/X_{2}).
why: Starting torque is non-zero.
R_{2} shifts the slip at maximum torque, not its value.
Torque is not linear with slip over the full range.

q: Starting torque of a slip-ring induction motor is maximum when rotor resistance per phase equals:
explanation: Maximum torque occurs at s = R_{2}/X_{2}; for it to occur at standstill (s = 1), R_{2} = X_{2}.
why: Stator resistance is not the controlling factor.
Beyond R_{2} = X_{2}, starting torque falls again.
Zero resistance gives low starting torque.

q: With a star-delta starter, starting line current compared with direct-on-line starting is:
explanation: Phase voltage falls to 1/√3, phase current to 1/√3, and line current in star equals phase current while in delta it is √3 × phase: overall ratio 1/3. Starting torque is also 1/3.
why: The starter exists to reduce it.
That is the phase-voltage ratio.
Current is reduced, not increased.

q: A motor draws 60 A when started direct-on-line. With a star-delta starter, starting line current is:
solution: Star-delta reduces starting line current to 1/3 of DOL
why: Divides by √3 only.
No reduction.
Multiplies instead.

q: If the supply voltage to an induction motor falls by 10%, its starting torque becomes about:
explanation: 81% of original
why: Torque depends on voltage.
Assumes T ∝ V.
Torque falls, not rises.

q: Rotor bars of a squirrel-cage motor are usually skewed to:
options: Reduce noise and prevent cogging (magnetic locking)
explanation: Skewing reduces slot harmonics, giving quieter operation and avoiding cogging/locking of rotor and stator teeth.
why: Slip is set by load and rotor resistance.
Skewing slightly increases bar length.
Not a design aim.

q: Crawling of an induction motor (running stably at about 1/7 of synchronous speed) is caused by:
explanation: The 7th space harmonic rotates forward at N_{s}/7 and can produce a torque dip where the motor “crawls”.
why: High rotor resistance increases starting torque.
The 5th harmonic rotates backward and causes a braking dip but not forward crawling at 1/7.
Unbalance causes heating and negative-sequence torque.

q: A single-phase induction motor is not self-starting because:
options: A single-phase winding produces a pulsating, not rotating, field
explanation: A pulsating field = two equal and opposite rotating fields; at standstill their torques cancel. An auxiliary winding with a capacitor creates a phase-shifted field to start it.
why: Not the cause.
Frequency is the normal 50 Hz.
It has a cage rotor.

q: A synchronous motor is:
explanation: The rotor cannot lock instantly onto a field rotating at N_{s}; average torque is zero. It is started with damper (amortisseur) windings as an induction motor, or by a pony motor.
why: It runs on AC.
Average torque at standstill is zero.
Load has nothing to do with it.

q: An over-excited synchronous motor running at no load and used for power factor correction is called a:
explanation: Over-excitation makes it draw leading current, so it supplies reactive power like a capacitor bank but with smooth control.
why: An induction generator absorbs reactive power.
Phase advancers improve pf of induction motors by rotor injection.
A converter changes AC to DC.

q: V-curves of a synchronous motor are plotted between:
options: Armature current and field current at constant load
explanation: Armature current is minimum at unity pf (normal excitation) and rises for under- (lagging) and over-excitation (leading), giving a V shape. Inverted V-curves plot pf against field current.
why: Speed is constant.
Torque–slip curves belong to induction motors.
Speed of a synchronous motor is constant.

q: Increasing the field excitation of an alternator connected to an infinite bus mainly changes its:
explanation: Excitation controls internal EMF, which changes reactive power (and pf). Real power is changed through the prime-mover input (governor).
why: Real power needs more turbine input.
Frequency is fixed by the infinite bus.
Speed is locked to synchronous speed.

q: Which condition is NOT required for paralleling an alternator with the bus bars?
explanation: Voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle must match (checked by synchroscope or lamps). Machines of different ratings are routinely paralleled.
why: Unequal voltage causes reactive circulating current.
Unequal frequency causes power swings.
Wrong sequence causes a short circuit.

q: Alternators for hydroelectric stations are generally:
explanation: Water turbines run slowly, so many poles are needed for 50 Hz; salient-pole rotors of large diameter and short axial length suit this. Steam/gas turbo-alternators are cylindrical-rotor 2/4-pole machines.
why: That describes turbo-alternators.
2-pole would need 3000 rpm.
Cylindrical rotors suit high speeds.

q: A hydro-generator runs at 300 rpm on a 50 Hz system. Number of poles is:
explanation: = 20 poles
why: That would need 250 rpm.
That would need 600 rpm.
That would need 500 rpm.

q: The most accurate method of finding the voltage regulation of an alternator is the:
options: Direct loading only for large machines
explanation: EMF method is pessimistic (over-estimates), MMF method optimistic; Potier/ZPF separates leakage reactance and armature reaction and is most accurate among indirect methods.
why: Optimistic: gives a lower regulation.
Direct loading is impractical for large machines.
Pessimistic: gives a higher regulation.

q: Damper windings in synchronous machines are used to:
explanation: Damper (amortisseur) bars carry induced currents only when speed deviates from synchronous, damping oscillations (hunting); they also give induction-motor starting torque.
why: Pf is controlled by excitation.
They add slight losses during transients.
They do not affect steady voltage.

q: Short-circuit ratio (SCR) of a synchronous machine is approximately equal to:
options: Reciprocal of saturated synchronous reactance in p.u.
Ratio of armature to field resistance
explanation: SCR = I_{f} for rated OC voltage / I_{f} for rated SC current ≈ 1/X_{s(pu)}. High SCR → smaller X_{s}, better stability and regulation but larger, costlier machine.
why: It is the reciprocal.
Resistances are not involved.
Leakage reactance is only part of X_{s}.
